drills.q: What are the three quantities that trade against each other?
options: Read, write and space amplification
Latency, throughput and durability
Reads, writes and deletes
Memory, disk and network
drills.why: Improving one worsens another, and the choice is which one your workload can afford to be bad at.

drills.q: A hundred-byte update to a B-tree with four kilobyte pages writes how much?
options: Four kilobytes, before the device's own amplification
A hundred bytes
A hundred bytes plus a journal record
It depends on how full the page is
drills.why: The page is the unit of update, so the amplification is forty and the device applies its own on top of that.

drills.q: Why is a B-tree lookup usually one device access rather than four?
options: The upper levels are small and touched by every lookup, so they stay cached
The tree has only one level in practice
The leaf holds the whole path
Lookups are batched
drills.why: The fanout makes the tree shallow and the interior levels tiny, so the leaf is the only part the cache cannot hold.

drills.q: What happens when a B-tree page fills?
options: It splits, rewriting two pages and an ancestor, possibly up to the root
It chains an overflow page
The tree is rebuilt in the background
The record goes to the next page
drills.why: Which is a rare event with a large cost, and it is why write latency in a B-tree has a long tail.

drills.q: In a log-structured tree, what does an update read from the device?
options: Nothing
The page the key currently lives in
The summary filter for that key
The most recent file
drills.why: An append to a log and an insertion into memory. Nothing on the device is read, and nothing on it is modified.

drills.q: Where does the log structure's write amplification actually come from?
options: Merging, which rewrites each record once per level it passes through
The durability log
The memory table flush alone
The summary filters
drills.why: It is deferred and batched rather than absent, which is the point: large sequential runs at the system's choosing, not small random writes at update time.

drills.q: A summary filter can answer which two ways?
options: Definitely not present, or possibly present
Definitely present, or possibly present
Present or absent, exactly
Present, absent, or deleted
drills.why: The one-sided error is what makes it useful and what makes it cheap: a negative skips the file entirely, and a positive costs a read that may find nothing.

drills.q: Ten bits per key gives roughly a one percent false positive rate. What does that buy across seven files?
options: A lookup for an absent key reads about one file rather than seven
A lookup reads no files at all
Reads become as fast as a B-tree's
The merge cost drops by a factor of seven
drills.why: It is the third amplification bought with the first: memory spent to avoid reads.

drills.q: Who does the filter not help?
options: A workload whose lookups mostly succeed
A workload checking for existence
A workload of range scans
A write-heavy workload
drills.why: A key that is present has to be read from the file holding it whatever the filters say, so the filter saves nothing on the path that matters.

drills.q: Why is a spinning disk a reasonable fit for a B-tree?
options: A random read and a random write both cost a seek, so the costs are symmetric
Disks have no write amplification
Disks are fast at small writes
Disks reorder writes into sequential runs
drills.why: The structure was designed for that machine. What changed was not the software.

drills.q: What is the log-structured design a response to?
options: A device whose write path is the expensive one
A device that is slow overall
Growing dataset sizes
The cost of memory
drills.why: It converts many small random writes into few large sequential ones, which is exactly the transformation that makes a flash controller's garbage collection cheap.

drills.q: What does a deletion do in a log-structured engine?
options: Writes a marker; the record stays until a merge removes both
Removes the record from its file
Marks the record's file for immediate merging
Frees the space at the next flush
drills.why: Nothing is modified in place, so a delete is another append. In a B-tree it is an update, and the space is immediately reusable.

drills.q: What does a workload of repeated inserts and deletes of the same keys accumulate?
options: Markers, faster than merging removes them
Free space
Deeper levels
Larger summary filters
drills.why: And a range that was emptied still has to be walked past, so scanning a mostly deleted region reads all the markers.

drills.q: Which structure does a range scan favour, and why?
options: The B-tree, because its leaves are already in order
The log structure, because its files are sorted
Neither; the cost is the same
The log structure, because scans are sequential there
drills.why: The log structure must read from every file the range overlaps and merge them on the fly, where the B-tree reads one contiguous run.

drills.q: Both families sit on a flushed log. What limits a system doing many small durable updates?
options: Flushes per second, which is why commits are grouped
The structure's write amplification
The size of the memory table
The summary filters' false positive rate
drills.why: The structure decides what the steady state costs and the log decides what a crash costs, and grouping trades a little latency for a great deal of throughput.
